content.title: About
content.content: Beef stew is a dish made from bite‑size pieces of beef slowly simmered in a flavorful broth with vegetables and spices. The long cooking time makes the meat tender and the sauce rich and aromatic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef stew is traditionally cooked in heavy‑bottomed pots that distribute heat evenly.
Many cultures have their own versions: French "boeuf bourguignon", Irish "stew", and Japanese "niku‑jiru".
Slow cooking helps retain most nutrients that can be lost with high‑heat frying.
Cuts with connective tissue, such as chuck or brisket, are ideal for stewing.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef stew supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc from beef supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Stewed meat contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Some beef cuts can be high in saturated fat; choosing lean cuts is recommended.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor harmful bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: A rare allergy to beef can cause reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, often with a side of potatoes, rice, or vegetables. Beef stew can also be added to soups, casseroles, or used as a filling for pies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the stew to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months.
